strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: whether semantic and acoustic information can be disentangled at the token level, with a clean architectural answer (parallel frozen semantic stream + trainable acoustic stream) that contrasts with prior 'X-shaped' fused designs

Comprehensive evaluation protocol covering reconstruction (STOI, PESQ, UTMOS, SIM, WER) and semantic representation (ARCH benchmark with SSL references), with many strong baselines reproduced from official checkpoints at comparable bitrates

Impressive empirical results: state-of-the-art reconstruction at both 875 and 525 bps, semantic representation approaching continuous SSL features, and robustness demonstrated on test-other under noisy conditions

The disentanglement analysis is a genuinely interesting contribution: semantic-only reconstruction achieves 3.99% WER versus SemantiCodec's 30.67%, and acoustic-only reconstruction is intelligible but semantically empty, supported by both quantitative metrics (WER, SIM, MSIM) and qualitative mel-spectrogram comparisons (Appendix D)
Useful ablations isolating the effect of speaker and semantic auxiliary supervision, with honest reporting of the small effect of removing semantic loss
Good transparency on training details, data composition, loss weights, and limitations section acknowledging the speech-only scope
Code and pre-trained models are stated to be released, plus a demo
weaknesses: Novelty is largely compositional: the semantic stream is a frozen off-the-shelf tokenizer (Zeng et al., 2024b, i.e., CosyVoice's S3 tokenizer), so the headline semantic performance is substantially inherited from prior work rather than learned; the paper's core contribution is the fusion and training recipe, which is competent but incremental relative to SemantiCodec and XY-Tokenizer

Potential evaluation bias: the semantic stream is derived from an ASR-supervised tokenizer, and the semantic evaluation relies on ASR-based WER and ARCH probing tasks (SLURP intent, AudioMNIST digits) that are strongly text-correlated; this metric suite plausibly favors their design choice, and no evaluation specifically probing limitations of ASR-aligned semantics is offered

No subjective listening evaluation (human MOS); UTMOS exceeding ground truth is explained as generative enhancement, but UTMOS is known to be unreliable for heavily generated speech, and claims of 'superior perceptual quality' rest on objective proxies alone

Bitrate comparisons are not tightly controlled: SAC at 875 bps is compared against baselines at 800-1040 bps, and SAC's dual-stream token rate (62.5 Hz) complicates like-for-like comparisons; some bolded 'best' claims depend on these fuzzy groupings

The ablation of L_sem shows almost no measurable effect (all metrics essentially unchanged), which weakens the narrative that the auxiliary semantic objective is important and leaves the source of SAC's semantic advantage under-explained

In-house training data (roughly 700 hours) is included; although the authors argue reproducibility is unaffected, this cannot be verified, and the code/model release links are empty placeholders in the submitted PDF
Ablations are run only in the low-bitrate configuration, and there is no ablation of the acoustic stream design choices (e.g., Encodec-based encoder, codebook size, frame rate trade-offs)

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across two bitrate regimes with a broad set of recent baselines (X-Codec2, XY-Tokenizer, SemantiCodec, BigCodec, Mimi, etc.) reproduced on a common test set, plus an additional noisy-condition evaluation (test-other) that most codec papers omit.

The dual-stream design is cleanly motivated and the disentanglement analysis (semantic-only vs. acoustic-only reconstruction, MSIM analysis, spectrogram visualizations including SpeechTokenizer RVQ-layer comparisons in Appendix D) provides direct, interpretable evidence for the core claim.

Ablation studies (speaker and semantic supervision, Tables 4-5) are present and the paper is generally well organized and clearly written, with training data statistics and loss configurations disclosed in the appendix.

Code and pre-trained models are stated to be released, supporting reproducibility, and the training corpus is largely composed of public datasets with the in-house portion small enough that the authors plausibly argue reproduction is feasible.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a straightforward combination of existing components — a frozen pre-trained semantic tokenizer (Zeng et al., 2024b), a DAC/Encodec-style acoustic stream, and a ConvNeXt prenet for fusion. The architecture is close to what SemantiCodec and XY-Tokenizer already explore, and the claim that this is 'the first instance of such a clean disentanglement' is overstated given prior decoupled and semantic-guided codecs.

Evaluation relies entirely on proxy metrics without any human listening test (MOS/CMOS). The reported UTMOS scores exceeding ground truth (4.25-4.27 vs. 4.09) strongly suggest the GAN decoder is gaming the neural MOS predictor rather than genuinely improving perceptual quality; this weakens the central 'superior perceptual quality' claim.

The strongest semantic-representation results (Table 3) are partly inherited rather than earned: the semantic stream is a frozen, externally pre-trained tokenizer, and the concatenated dual-stream representation is compared against single-stream codecs at pooled level, which is not an apples-to-apples comparison of representation quality.

No downstream SLM experiments (TTS, ASR via LLM, spoken dialogue) are provided, so the practical benefit of the dual tokens for the motivating use case is asserted but never demonstrated; the evaluation stops at probing benchmarks (ARCH), which the authors themselves admit may be too coarse (global pooling).

Ablation results undercut the method's own narrative: removing the semantic loss (w/o L_sem) changes essentially nothing (Table 4), yet Section 5.3 frames the semantic supervision as important; similarly, the semantic-only comparison in Table 5 pairs SAC at 175 bps against SemantiCodec at 750 bps, an unbalanced comparison.

Some bitrate comparisons appear favorable to SAC (e.g., 875 bps vs. X-Codec2's 800 bps in Table 1; 525 bps vs. TS3-Codec's 680 bps in Table 2), and model size, inference speed, and streaming capability are not reported for baselines, limiting the fairness of the 'state-of-the-art' claims.

The loss-coefficient section gives fixed values (e.g., λ_sem = 1000) with no sensitivity analysis, and the very large weight suggests the semantic loss dominates training, which deserves more scrutiny given its ablation shows no effect.

strengths: The proposed dual-stream semantic-acoustic codec is clearly motivated: disentangling semantic and acoustic modeling into separate frozen-tokenizer and codec streams directly addresses a known limitation of fused semantic-acoustic codecs, and the design is well described and easy to follow.

Evaluation is unusually comprehensive for a codec paper: two bitrate settings, many strong and recent baselines (DAC, Mimi, BigCodec, X-Codec 1/2, XY-Tokenizer, SemantiCodec, MagiCodec, etc.), noisy-condition robustness (test-other), and a semantic-representation evaluation (ARCH) with SSL references.

Results are strong and consistent across bitrates: WER close to ground truth, UTMOS above ground truth, and large gains over the second-best codec on ARCH (~10%), with informative per-task analysis (semantic stream drives SLURP/AudioMNIST, acoustic stream drives emotion recognition).

The disentanglement analysis (semantic-only and acoustic-only reconstruction, WER/SIM/MSIM, mel-spectrogram comparisons against SemantiCodec and SpeechTokenizer) provides genuine insight and evidence for the central claim that the two streams are cleanly separated.

Ablations of the auxiliary speaker and semantic supervision losses are included, and training details (datasets, loss weights, optimizer, codebook sizes, model size) are reported in sufficient depth to support reproduction; code and pre-trained models are stated to be released.
weaknesses: No human listening tests (subjective MOS) are reported. Claims of 'superior perceptual quality' rest entirely on UTMOS, and UTMOS exceeding ground truth is a well-known signature of generative enhancement rather than faithful reconstruction, which weakens the perceptual-quality claim.

The semantic stream is a frozen, pre-existing tokenizer from Zeng et al. (2024b). Since SAC_sem largely inherits the semantic capability of that tokenizer, the headline claim that SAC's semantic representation is 'comparable to SSL models' partly reflects the adopted component rather than the proposed contribution; a comparison against the raw Zeng et al. tokenizer itself would clarify what SAC adds.

The ablation showing removing L_sem has almost no effect (Table 4) is in tension with the paper's framing: it supports robustness of the dual-stream design but undercuts the necessity of the semantic auxiliary objective, and this deserves deeper discussion.

Bitrate comparisons are not fully controlled (e.g., SAC at 875 BPS versus BigCodec at 1040 BPS, or XY-Tokenizer at 1000 BPS), and the term 'state-of-the-art' is applied to wins at comparable-but-unequal operating points; results are also confined to a single evaluation set (LibriSpeech) without significance testing.

Downstream utility in actual SLM applications (TTS, speech understanding, dialogue) is not demonstrated; evidence is limited to probing benchmarks and reconstruction WER, so claims about 'new potential for controllable speech applications' remain speculative.
Training uses ~730 hours of in-house bilingual data, which somewhat limits exact reproducibility, and some links in the abstract/footnotes (demo, code) appear broken in the manuscript.

The methodological novelty is relatively incremental: the main components (frozen semantic tokenizer, DAC-style single-codebook acoustic stream, ConvNeXt prenet, speaker-feature MSE supervision) are individually established; the contribution is primarily their combination and the empirical demonstration that this combination disentangles cleanly.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-organized evaluation: reconstruction across clean and noisy conditions at multiple bitrates (Tables 1, 2, 7, 8), semantic probing on the ARCH benchmark (Table 3), auxiliary-loss ablations (Tables 4, 13), downstream LLM-based TTS (Table 9), subjective MOS (Table 10), data-scale analysis (Table 11), and RTF/efficiency analysis (Table 12).

The dual-stream design (frozen semantic tokenizer + learned acoustic codec) yields strong and consistent results: near-ground-truth WER at low bitrates, large gains over prior codecs on ARCH (e.g., ~10% over XY-Tokenizer), and competitive single-stage AR TTS on Seed-TTS-eval.

The disentanglement analysis (semantic-only and acoustic-only reconstruction, Table 5 and Figs. 3-4) is a genuinely interesting finding with clear quantitative support (low SIM of 0.17, high MSIM, WER 3.99 vs. SemantiCodec's 30.67), and suggests applications such as speaker anonymization and controllable generation.

Good attention to fairness concerns: SACsmall trained only on LibriSpeech shows the approach works at small data scale, and the appendix transparently reports hyperparameters, loss weights, training data statistics, and acknowledges in-house data limitations.

Clarity of presentation is high, with a well-motivated research question (can semantic and acoustic tokens be disentangled at the token level?) positioned against related 'X-shaped' fusion approaches.
Code and pre-trained models are stated to be released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the architecture is largely a composition of existing components (a frozen pre-trained semantic tokenizer from Zeng et al. 2024b, an Encodec/DAC-style acoustic codec, ConvNeXt prenet, standard VQ-GAN losses). The main delta over prior disentangling work (SemantiCodec, Mimi, SpeechTokenizer) is freezing a supervised semantic tokenizer rather than distilling it, which is more an engineering insight than a new technique.

Potential evaluation circularity for WER: the semantic stream derives from a tokenizer trained under ASR supervision, and reconstruction WER is measured with a HuBERT-based ASR model; this may favor SAC relative to codecs whose semantics are not ASR-aligned. The paper does not discuss this bias.

Part of the semantic-representation claim is inherited: SACsem (Table 3) largely measures the frozen pre-trained tokenizer, so the codec's own contribution to semantic performance needs more careful attribution; concatenating streams before linear probing on ARCH further blurs which stream drives which result (the paper acknowledges the global-pooling limitation only briefly).

TTS baselines (Spark-TTS, Llasa) are cited from their original papers rather than re-evaluated under identical conditions, weakening the 'clearly outperforms SOTA AR systems' claim; the SAC model also uses a different backbone (Qwen3-0.6B) and data distribution, complicating attribution of gains to the tokenizer.

In-house training data cannot be fully reproduced, and the diversity/balancing procedure (VoxBox-style annotation) is only sketched; the ablation that removing semantic supervision barely changes results (Table 4) slightly undercuts the necessity of one of the proposed auxiliary losses.

Some claims are stated more strongly than the evidence (e.g., 'first instance of such a clean disentanglement', UTMOS exceeding ground truth attributed to decoder generative behavior) without deeper analysis or listening-test confirmation of those specific phenomena.

strengths: The paper is empirically thorough: reconstruction is evaluated at two bitrates against a wide range of recent codecs (Tables 1-2), with additional noisy-condition evaluations (Tables 7-8), a subjective MOS study (Table 10), data-scale ablations (Table 11), inference-speed measurements (Table 12), and spectrogram visualizations across codecs (Figures 3-4).

The core idea—freezing a pre-trained semantic tokenizer and adding an independent acoustic stream rather than fusing streams before quantization—is clearly motivated, and the disentanglement analysis (Table 5, MSIM of 0.64 with SIM of 0.17 under semantic-only reconstruction) provides direct, quantitative evidence for the central claim rather than relying only on aggregate metrics.

The ARCH representation evaluation (Table 3) shows the codec's semantic representations approach continuous SSL features, a meaningful result for token-based speech LMs, and the finding that the acoustic stream contributes ~20% on emotion recognition while the semantic stream dominates text-related tasks supports the disentanglement story.

Downstream validation is substantive rather than token: a 100k-hour AR TTS model built on SAC tokens outperforms Spark-TTS and Llasa on Seed-TTS-eval (Table 9), demonstrating the tokens are usable for LLM-based generation, not just reconstruction.

Reproducibility is addressed reasonably well: training data composition is detailed (Appendix A, Table 6), hyperparameters and loss weights are given (Appendix B), baselines are reproduced on a shared test set using official checkpoints, and code and pre-trained models are stated to be released.

The ablation of auxiliary supervision (Tables 4, 13) is informative and honest—it shows the dual-stream design, not the auxiliary losses, drives semantic quality, and the authors openly recommend simplifications for resource-constrained settings.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is moderate: the semantic stream is a frozen, pre-existing tokenizer (Zeng et al., 2024b) used essentially off-the-shelf, the acoustic stream follows Encodec/DAC conventions, and the decoder follows X-Codec patterns. The contribution is primarily a system-level combination and empirical demonstration, which limits the conceptual advance relative to SemantiCodec and XY-Tokenizer.

Some headline claims are stronger than the evidence: 'SOTA performance' is asserted largely on LibriSpeech test-clean reconstructions and ARCH probing, and the claim of being 'the first instance of such a clean disentanglement' rests on comparisons with only two prior decoupled codecs (SemantiCodec, SpeechTokenizer).

The TTS comparison (Table 9) cites baseline numbers from the Spark-TTS and Llasa papers rather than re-running them, and the comparison is confounded by differences in backbone size (Qwen3-0.6B vs. Qwen2.5-0.5B and Llama-3.2-1B), training data, and token rate; the paper's attribution of the SIM drop to token rate is plausible but not experimentally isolated.

Evaluation coverage is narrow in places: reconstruction is on LibriSpeech only, and the paper itself acknowledges that the global-pooling ARCH protocol may not distinguish finer-grained representation differences; language coverage of the tokenizer's ASR-based semantics raises questions about generalization beyond Chinese/English, which the Limitations section flags but does not test.

UTMOS scores exceeding ground truth (4.25-4.27 vs. 4.09; 3.84/3.90 vs. 3.50 on test-other) are explained by the decoder acting as a generative enhancer, but this also means UTMOS is partly measuring the decoder's generative prior rather than reconstruction fidelity—an issue the paper notes but does not fully control for.
The MOS study (20 listeners, 30 utterances) is small, and no confidence intervals or statistical significance are reported for any quantitative comparison.
A small amount of in-house training data is used; while the authors argue its impact is negligible, this is asserted rather than demonstrated, which slightly weakens full reproducibility.

The interleaved flattening scheme for downstream LLM modeling (Appendix D) is described as 'novel' but is only sketched and not ablated, so its contribution to the TTS gains versus the tokenizer itself is unclear.

strengths: The core idea—disentangling semantic and acoustic tokenization into two parallel, independently quantized streams rather than fusing semantic supervision into a single token stream—is clearly motivated and addresses a genuine, well-documented tension in speech tokenizers for language modeling.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for a codec paper: reconstruction at two bitrates (Tables 1-2), noisy-condition robustness (test-other, Tables 7-8), semantic probing on ARCH against both codec and SSL baselines (Table 3), auxiliary-loss ablations (Tables 4, 13), a semantic-only/acoustic-only disentanglement analysis with both quantitative metrics (Table 5) and spectrogram visualizations (Figs. 3-4), MOS with 20 raters (Table 10), data-scale analysis (Table 11), and RTF efficiency measurements (Table 12).

Downstream validation is substantive: a single-stage AR TTS model trained on 100k hours achieves very low WER/CER and UTMOS on Seed-TTS-eval, outperforming Spark-TTS and Llasa despite using a smaller backbone and less training data, which supports the practical value of the tokenizer beyond reconstruction.

Reproducibility is supported by detailed training configurations (loss weights, optimizer, codebook sizes, strides, EMA, pretraining schedule), public data sources with per-dataset statistics, an analysis showing reproduction with open-source data should be feasible, and a stated code/model release.

The ablations isolate the contributions of the dual-stream design itself (the semantic stream remains robust when L_sem is removed, unlike X-shaped codecs), the speaker supervision (clear SIM gain at minor PESQ cost), and the disentanglement claim is directly evidenced (SIM 0.17 / MSIM 0.64 in semantic-only decoding, plus qualitative spectrogram comparisons against SemantiCodec and SpeechTokenizer).
weaknesses: The semantic stream is a frozen, pre-trained tokenizer from prior work (Zeng et al., 2024b); the acoustic stream is an Encodec/DAC-derived design with established techniques. The novelty is therefore primarily architectural composition (parallel streams plus a fusion prenet) rather than a new tokenization mechanism, and part of the strong semantic performance is inherited rather than learned.

Some headline comparisons are not fully controlled: the low-bitrate SAC operates at 525 bps / 37.5 Hz versus several baselines at 480-850 bps; TTS results in Table 9 are cited from other papers rather than reproduced, with differing backbones (Qwen3-0.6B vs. Llama-3.2-1B vs. Qwen2.5-0.5B) and potentially differing WER evaluation pipelines, which weakens the claim of clearly surpassing SOTA AR systems.

The claim of 'first instance of such a clean disentanglement' relies on a single qualitative construct (semantic-only reconstruction); the ARCH probing protocol uses global average pooling, which the authors themselves acknowledge may mask finer-grained differences, and no quantitative information-theoretic or mutual-information measure of disentanglement is provided.

UTMOS exceeding the ground-truth score is interpreted favorably (the decoder 'acts as a generator'), but this conflates codec reconstruction fidelity with generative enhancement; the paper would benefit from more careful discussion of whether reconstruction is the right frame for such metrics.

Minor presentation issues: an internal cross-reference error ('As shown in Figure 12' should be Table 12 in Appendix G), a missing URL after 'available at' on page 1 (appears blank), and scattered attribution of performance to architectural hypotheses ('we hypothesize...') without direct supporting experiments.

Generalization beyond speech (music, sound events) is unaddressed, which limits the scope of a codec contribution in a landscape where general-audio codecs are increasingly expected; the limitations section acknowledges this but it remains a substantive gap relative to baselines like SemantiCodec.
